title: The Bus in the Parking Lot
part: PART ONE: EIGHT GAMES, ZERO WINS

pages.text:
*Way to Lose #7: Meet a new coach and decide in ten seconds that she's not the answer.*

Tuesday practice is usually a ghost town, with brown grass and mud cracked like a dry riverbed while the wind whistles through the chain-link fence. I stand on the center circle holding the ball, waiting for a coach who will never come.

Then the ground shakes. A low, rumbling moan rolls across the field, vibrating through my cleats and up into my teeth. I look up to see a yellow school bus, dented on the left side and covered in dust, rolling slowly into the Marigold Park lot. It moves with the heavy, deliberate grace of a turtle trying to cross the playground, stopping right in front of the dugout with the engine sputtering once before sighing into silence.

The side door slides open. A boot steps down, followed by another.

I squint at the figure emerging from the vehicle. It is not a person in a tracksuit, and it is certainly not a person in a windbreaker. It is a person who looks like she belongs on the bus.

I grip the ball until my knuckles turn white. I have eight games of zero wins to explain, and my stomach is doing a slow roll downhill, like a marble trapped in a broken jar.
pages.image: A big blank yellow minibus parked in a muddy suburban lot near a soccer field, side door open, one boot on the ground, dust rising, empty parking area, overcast sky, quiet mood.

pages.text:
The woman climbs down the steps. She is short and square, with a silver braid pulled back tight. Sunglasses rest on top of her head. She wears a fluorescent yellow windbreaker that looks like it has seen better decades. On her neck hangs a lanyard with a whistle and a bus key. In her hand is a steel thermos, dented and serious.

She walks to the field. She looks at the muddy pitch. She looks at the duck pond, where three ducks are preening their feathers. She looks at the team, who are standing in a row, nervous and silent.

She does not say "Hello." She does not say "Let's win."

She takes a long sip from the thermos, wipes her mouth with her thumb, and says, "Well. That's a lot of information."

I blink. I wait for the other shoe to drop. It does not. She turns to the ducks. "You guys see that too, right?"

A duck honks. She nods, satisfied.
pages.image: A short woman with a silver braid and sunglasses on her head, wearing a bright yellow windbreaker, holding a steel thermos, standing on a muddy soccer field looking at a duck pond, small team in background, calm atmosphere.

pages.text:
She walks down the line without asking for names, demanding details instead.

To Tank, who is fidgeting with his cleats, she asks, "What did you have for breakfast?"
"Three pancakes," he says, then adds, "I'm sorry, I didn't mean to eat them all."
"Good," she says.

To Josie, who is mid-sentence about her dog's haircut, she holds up a hand. "Stop. Count to ten."
Josie stops. "One, two, three, four, five, six."
"Good," Gin says. "Six is enough."

To Ahmed, who is leaning against a cone, she asks, "What do you do when you have the ball?"
"Run," he says.
"And the rest of the team?"
He shrugs. "They're slow."

Gin turns to Priya. "Priya. What do you see?"
Priya opens her mouth. Her voice is a whisper, barely a breath.
Gin waits. She does not ask her to repeat it. She just nods, as if the silence itself was the answer.
pages.image: A group of young soccer players standing on a muddy field, a short woman in a yellow windbreaker talking to them, one large boy looking shy, a girl whispering, a boy leaning against a cone, casual interaction, bright daylight.

pages.text:
It is my turn. I am the captain, which means I have a job to do, so I step forward with my yellow armband tight on my arm.

"Coach," I start, my voice cracking slightly. "We are last. We have lost eight games. We have let in fifty-one goals. There is a video of me scoring an own goal that is on every phone in school. We are a disaster."

I am still talking. I am listing the failures, the statistics, and the pain, trying to give her the full weight of the situation so she understands why I am holding my breath.

*Blow.*

The whistle cuts through the air like a sharp, singular note. I stop.

Gin looks at me. Her face is calm. She has not blinked.

"I didn't ask what the scoreboard says," she says. Her voice is flat, steady. "I asked who's on my team."

I open my mouth to argue, to explain the difference, but the words die in my throat. I look down at my cleats. The green and orange laces are tangled. I do not know who I am if I am not the scoreboard.
pages.image: A girl in a yellow armband standing nervously on a soccer field, a short woman in a yellow windbreaker holding a whistle, looking at the girl with a calm expression, muddy ground, tense but quiet mood.

pages.text:
"Gather round," Gin says. She points at the bus. "Get on."

We climb the steps, our cleats thumping against the metal treads. The seats are hard and yellow, and the windows are open, letting in the smell of rain and cut grass. She pulls a cord, and a small TV screen flickers to life above the driver's seat.

On the screen: game eight. Me. The own goal.

I stare. I have watched that clip a hundred times, but never from this angle. I see Priya close her eyes tight, squeezing them until her eyelids turn red. I see Ahmed leave his position, running and running, seven times. I see myself. I never look up. I keep my head down, staring at the grass, as if the ground will swallow me whole.

Gin taps the screen. "Look at the angles. Look at the eyes. Now. That's data."

The bus engine rumbles. I am sitting in the driver's seat of a vehicle that has been to a thousand places, and for the first time, I do not feel like I am alone in the mud.
